name: Chin-Up

inherit.why: true for this child because the lifter is still what falls if the hand opens, and ACE's chin-up setup itself asks for thumbs wrapped (c1, c21); parent c3.

inherit.field: zooms.hand (full grip, thumb around the bar, is the only grip shown)
inherit.why: true for this child because the thumb rule on a hang does not depend on palm direction (parent zoom 'hand' and c3; content.md 5.2 C4).

claims.text: ACE sets up the chin-up with the palms facing you and a full grip, thumbs wrapped around the bar.

quotes.text: reach your arms overhead with your palms facing you. Reach, jump or lift your body off the floor to grasp the handles firmly with a full grip position (thumbs wrapped around the handles).

claims.text: Coaching sources put the hands about shoulder-width apart, or slightly closer, for the chin-up.

quotes.text: Grip the bar with a supinated grip (palms facing you), about shoulder-width apart.
A chin-up uses a supinated grip (palms facing the client), typically shoulder-width or slightly closer, and involves shoulder extension.

claims.text: ACE asks for a neutral wrist: the wrist in a straight line with the forearm.

quotes.text: assume a neutral wrist position (i.e., wrist aligned in a straight line with your forearms).

claims.text: Before the arms bend, the shoulder blades are pulled down and back, and that position is held for the whole set.

quotes.text: Depress and retract your scapulae (pull shoulders back and down) and attempt to hold this position throughout the exercise.
Set the scapulae first, cueing 'pull the shoulder blades down and back' before the arms take over, so the client leads with the back rather than yanking with the arms.

claims.text: The pull drives the elbows straight down toward the floor while they stay in front of the body.

quotes.text: Attempt to pull in a motion that drives your elbows directly down towards the floor, keeping your elbows in front of your body.

claims.text: The body stays vertical without swinging; kipping, partial range and craning the neck are the named faults.

quotes.text: Attempt to keep your body aligned vertically to the floor and avoid swinging your body during your upward pull
Discourage the common faults: kipping and momentum on strict-strength work, partial range of motion (coach a full hang at the bottom to a chin-clearing top), and craning the neck.

claims.text: The rep ends when the chin is level with the bar, pauses briefly, and returns slowly to fully straight arms.

quotes.text: Continue pulling upward until your chin is level with the bar or your hands. Pause momentarily then slowly return to your starting position by allowing your arms to extend back overhead until your arms are fully extended.

claims.text: ACE describes a slow pull, a brief pause at the top and a slow return. It gives no seconds, so the 2-1-2 count on the plate is a drawing convention, not a sourced number.

quotes.text: Slowly exhale and slowly pull your body upwards by flexing (bending) your elbows
Pause momentarily then slowly return to your starting position

claims.text: ACE has the lifter gently cross one leg over the other and brace the abs to keep the lower body still.

quotes.text: Gently cross one leg over the other to stabilize your lower extremity and then stiffen ("brace") your abdominal muscles to stabilize your spine.

claims.text: Measured with EMG, the chin-up worked the biceps and the chest muscle harder than the pull-up, and the lower trapezius less.

quotes.text: The pectoralis major and biceps brachii had significantly higher EMG activation during the chin-up than during the pull-up, whereas the lower trapezius was significantly more active during the pull-up.

claims.text: Across the pull-up, chin-up and a rotating-handle version, the lats were the most active muscle, then the biceps; the lower trapezius and chest worked moderately.

quotes.text: latissimus dorsi (117-130%), biceps brachii (78-96%), infraspinatus (71-79%), lower trapezius (45-56%), pectoralis major (44-57%)

claims.text: In an ACE-funded EMG study of eight back exercises, the pull-up and the chin-up activated the lats most.

quotes.text: Latissimus dorsi (Figure 3): The pull-up and chin-up had significantly greater muscle activation than the other six exercises.

claims.text: Prinold and Bull measured shoulder-blade motion in three pull-up styles; the palms-facing-posterior ('reverse') style showed extreme upper-arm rotation, a pattern they link to impingement risk. Reading 'palms facing posterior' with the arms overhead as the chin-up grip is this writer's interpretation.

quotes.text: palms facing anterior, palms facing posterior and wide-grip
The reverse technique has extreme glenohumeral internal-external rotation and large deviation from the scapula plane.
Wide and reverse pull-ups demonstrate kinematics patterns linked with increased impingement risk.

claims.text: With the arms high overhead, the space under the shoulder roof gets smaller, which the authors link to impingement risk.

quotes.text: High arm elevation during pull-ups reduces sub-acromial space and increases pressure, increasing the risk of impingement injury.

claims.text: In a modelling study the chin-up and pull-up gave the highest spine load of the pulling exercises tested, even though the body hangs.

quotes.text: The chin-up and pull-up exercises created the highest spine load as they required the highest muscle activation, despite the body "hanging" under tractioning gravitational load.

claims.text: NASM warns to progress gradually to avoid elbow overuse, and to send persistent shoulder or elbow pain, numbness or tingling to a professional instead of training through it.

quotes.text: progress gradually to avoid overuse issues like elbow tendon irritation
if a client reports shoulder or elbow pain, numbness, or tingling that persists, refer them to a physician or physical therapist rather than training through it.

claims.text: If a full chin-up is not possible yet, band or machine assistance and slow lowering-only reps build toward it.

quotes.text: Band-assisted reps or an assisted pull-up machine to practice the full pattern with reduced load.
Eccentric (negative) reps: jump or step to the top, then lower slowly

claims.text: At the bottom you hang freely with the elbows fully straight and the head between the arms.

quotes.text: Be sure to freely hang at the bottom of the chin-up. You should be able to have your head in between your biceps with the elbows fully extended.

claims.text: Grip and forearm strength are needed to hold the bar for the whole set.

quotes.text: A strong grip and forearms are needed to both keep you holding on to the bar itself as well as provide a stable connection to pull from.

claims.text: In 20 healthy adults squeezing a hand dynamometer, grip was strongest with the wrist in the position they chose themselves (about 35 degrees bent back) and weaker when the wrist was moved 10 to 15 degrees away from it in any direction, including curled forward (flexion). Applied to holding a bar or handle by reasoning, not measured on this exercise.

quotes.text: Grip strength and wrist position were recorded in the self-selected position and then again while the subjects voluntarily deviated the wrist randomly into flexion, extension, or radial or ulnar deviation of 10 to 15 degrees.
The self-selected position was 35 degrees of extension and 7 degrees of ulnar deviation.
Grip strength was significantly less in any position of deviation from this self-selected position, even after accounting for fatigue.

claims.text: NSCA-editor textbook guidance is to perform all grips with the thumbs around the bar. Written for barbell lifts (a drill lifting a bar from the floor); applied to the chin-up bar by inference.

quotes.text: Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar.

claims.text: ACE keeps the head in line with the trunk, under the hands.

quotes.text: Align your head vertically with your trunk under your hands

claims.text: NASM's progression is more reps, then less assistance, then added load; once reps come easily, load is added with a belt or dumbbell.

quotes.text: Apply progressive overload deliberately, more reps, less assistance, then added load
once reps come easily, added load via a belt or dumbbell for continued overload

claims.text: Starting the pull with the shoulders up by the ears (the shrug) is a named fault on the assisted pull-up machine; applied to the chin-up by inference, since no chin-up source names it.

quotes.text: The Shrug: Initiating the pull with your shoulders up by your ears.

claims.text: Hand contact: a manufacturer blog says that when you hang, the bar sits just below the base of the fingers, where the fingers meet the palm. Written for a palms-away hang (a callus blog) and applied to the chin-up by inference; weak evidence.

quotes.text: When you hang, the bar should sit just below the base of your fingers—where your fingers meet your palm.

sources.title: ACE-Sponsored Research: What Is the Best Back Exercise? (Edelburg, Porcari, Camic, Kovacs, Foster, with Green; ACE Certified, December 2018)
Grip selection and location, excerpt from Weight Training: Steps to Success, 5th ed. (Baechle and Earle, Human Kinetics)
Muscle activity and spine load during pulling exercises: influence of stable and labile contact surfaces and technique coaching (McGill, Cannon, Andersen, J Electromyogr Kinesiol)
Chin-Ups vs. Pull-Ups: A Trainer's Guide to Programming Both (NASM blog)
The relationship between wrist position, grasp size, and grip strength (O'Driscoll et al., J Hand Surg Am)
Scapula kinematics of pull-up techniques: Avoiding impingement risk with training changes (Prinold and Bull, J Sci Med Sport)
How to Do Chin-Up: Muscles Worked & Proper Form (StrengthLog)
Surface electromyographic activation patterns and elbow joint motion during a pull-up, chin-up, or perfect-pullup rotational exercise (Youdas et al., J Strength Cond Res)
How to Use a Pull-Up Assist Machine Correctly (Beginner's Guide) (Bullbar Fit, manufacturer blog)
How to Grip the Bar Without Getting Calluses (Bullbar Fit, manufacturer blog)

plate.equipment: Fixed overhead pull-up bar and floor line, as the pull_up plate. Feet clear the floor with straight arms.
plate.start: Free hang: elbows fully straight, arms overhead with the head between them (c18); palms toward the face, full grip (c1); shoulder blades set down and back (c4); legs crossed and still, body vertical under the bar (c9, c6); head in line with the trunk (c22).
plate.end: Chin level with the bar (c7); elbows driven down toward the floor and still in front of the body (c5); body still vertical, no leg kick (c6).

checkpoints.label: Shoulders set
checkpoints.what: Shoulder blades pulled down and back before the arms bend, held all set.

checkpoints.label: Elbows in front
checkpoints.what: Elbows drive straight down toward the floor and stay in front of the body.

checkpoints.label: Chin to bar
checkpoints.what: Pull until the chin is level with the bar, then lower to fully straight arms.

mistake.what: Swinging or kipping: the legs kick forward and the body arcs to throw the chin over the bar.
mistake.why: ACE and NASM both name swinging and kipping as the fault to avoid. How often it happens is not measured.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: no frequency word for a chin-up fault (curl and efetch 2026-10-18 of every read source). Set aside: "Many people are slightly stronger in this variation" (strengthlog-chin-up) and "chin-ups tend to feel easier for most clients" (nasm-chin-pull) are about strength, not a fault; "many lifters will find they can use significantly more load with the underhand row" (barbend-chin-up) is another exercise; bullbar-calluses' "Most people grab the bar like they're trying to strangle it." is a grip on a general bar-hang page and "Here's where most people go wrong: they hang from their shoulders like a sack of potatoes." is written for hanging in general, to prevent calluses, not for the chin-up. LR-31 step 2: two named faults are tied to harm, both on NASM's common-faults list (c6), one source each, both written for chin-ups: kipping (barbend-chin-up: "Kipping, when performed improperly, can end up placing high amounts of strain and stress on the connective tissues of the elbow and shoulder.") and partial range (nasm-chin-pull: "Quality reps through a full range build strength and protect the shoulder."). Two lists name both: NASM's, written for chin-ups and pull-ups, puts kipping and momentum first; Bullbar's, written for the assisted machine (c24, applied by inference), puts the partial rep first. Following LR-31's list order (the one written for this exercise first), NASM's list decides: swinging or kipping (c6) stays the pick. Set aside: NASM's "pulls carry injury risk when rushed" is about progression (its injury-prevention section), not a named rep fault; ACE's "Follow the instructions provided to reduce the stress placed upon your shoulder" names no fault; Prinold's reverse-grip impingement link (c13) is about the grip.

tells.text: Arms fully straight at the bottom

grip.type: Underhand (supinated), palms facing you, full closed grip.
grip.width: About shoulder-width apart, or slightly closer.
grip.thumb: Wrapped around the bar (c1, c21; inherited from pull_up, parent c3).
grip.handContact: Bar just below the base of the fingers, where the fingers meet the palm (c25).
grip.wrist: Straight, in line with the forearm (c3); not curled forward (c20).

setup.step: Stand under the bar, reach up with your palms facing you and take a full grip, thumbs wrapped.
Set your hands about shoulder-width apart, or slightly closer.
Keep your wrists straight, in line with your forearms.
Hang, gently cross one leg over the other and brace your abs.
Pull your shoulders down and back before you bend your arms.

posture.point: Free hang at the bottom: elbows fully straight, head between the arms.
Shoulder blades down and back, held for the whole set.
Elbows drive down toward the floor, in front of the body.
Body vertical and still: no swing, no kip.
Chin level with the bar at the top.
Head aligned with the trunk, under the hands.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Swinging, kicking or kipping to get the chin over the bar.
handlingMistakes.fix: Cross your legs, brace, keep the body vertical. If you can't finish a rep without swinging, use a band or the assisted machine, or do slow lowering-only reps; then build up with more reps, less assistance, then added load.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Half reps: stopping short of the bar, or not straightening the arms at the bottom.
handlingMistakes.fix: Go from a free hang with straight arms to chin level with the bar, every rep.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Starting the pull with the shoulders up by the ears.
handlingMistakes.fix: Pull your shoulders down and back first, then bend your arms.

rows.means: Expected: palms toward you make the biceps work harder than on a pull-up.

rows.where: Tops of the shoulders and neck
rows.means: Fault: starting the pull with your shoulders up by your ears.
rows.fix: Set your shoulders down and back before each rep.

rows.means: Arms high overhead narrow the space under the shoulder roof.
rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.

rows.means: Usually means too much pulling volume, too soon.
rows.fix: Build up the sets slowly. Don't train through the pain.

risks.risk: Shoulder: arms high overhead narrow the space under the shoulder roof, and the palms-toward-you style shows more upper-arm rotation.
Spine: chin-ups and pull-ups gave the highest spine load of the pulls tested, despite the hang.
Elbow overuse when volume rises too fast.

zooms.right: Palm facing the face, bar just below the base of the fingers, thumb wrapped around the bar, wrist straight in line with the forearm.
Shoulder blades pulled down and back before the arms bend.
zooms.wrong: Shoulders shrugged to the ears at the start of the pull.

zooms.right: Legs crossed and still, body vertical under the bar.
zooms.wrong: Legs kicking forward in an arc to throw the chin up.

add.why: Holding full body weight on the bar loads the grip (coach consensus, c19).

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json already lists lats and biceps as primary, which the chin-up EMG supports (c10, c11). mid_back stands: the lower trapezius works moderately (c11), folded into mid_back as on the pull_up card. Chest (pectoralis major, c10) is not added: a design choice to keep the feel list to the back and arm targets; the EMG shows it works (c10).

gaps: Tier A: no sourced way to get down from the bar or fail a rep safely (dismount); left out, not invented.
Tier A: safeties/J-hooks and bar path clear of the neck do not apply (bodyweight hang). Load progression is on handlingMistakes[0] (c17, c23); how much load to add, and when, is not sourced.

Tier A: no sourced line that the bar is fixed and dry or high enough for the feet to clear the floor; the pull_up card does not source them, and catalyst-pullup and bullbar-calluses do not say them (LR-34). Left out, not invented.
notes: Not sourced, so left out: a safe way down from the bar (the tier-A 'way out'); bar height, a fixed and dry bar, and chalk are not on the pull_up card, so none is inherited (LR-34): chalk is sourced by bullbar-calluses but the setup has no free slot (5 of 5 steps), and catalyst-pullup and bullbar-calluses do not say the bar is fixed or dry or how high it is; all three are in gaps. No source compares shoulder-width and closer chin-up grips. Prinold 2016 is read from the abstract only; the reverse = chin-up mapping is interpretation (c13). The StrengthLog chin-up page was re-fetched on 2026-09-30 (access full, quotes verbatim). The shrug fault is borrowed from the assisted-machine source (c24, WEAK). Wrist: the straight, in-line wrist comes from ACE (c3). O'Driscoll (c20) found the strongest dynamometer grip near 35 degrees of extension, so it does not support 'straight'; it is cited only for 'not curled forward' (zoom wrong, grip.wrist).

W2A LR-8 check redone under LR-34 against cards/pull_up.json on 5036283d (golden-B research is a source map only): the thumb holds (parent c3; c1 and c21 here) and the hand zoom's full-grip-only rule holds (parent zoom 'hand', c3; content.md 5.2 C4), each restating a whole string of tools/plates/layers/exercises/pull_up.howto.mjs on main. The thumbless, hook and gymnastics false-grip labels fail: the parent's baechle-earle quote gives only "Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar." (c3). Hand contact, bar height, a fixed and dry bar, and chalk fail because the parent card does not source them; those inherit entries are removed. Way (1): hand contact is this card's own c25 (bullbar-calluses, MECH, WEAK); chalk is sourced by bullbar-calluses but the setup has no free slot; catalyst-pullup and bullbar-calluses do not say the bar is fixed or dry or how high it is. Chalk, bar height and a fixed bar are in gaps.

W2A 2026-10-17: searched PubMed esearch 'pull-up AND (dismount OR fall OR falling)' (14 hits), 'chin-up AND injury' (5), 'horizontal bar AND fall AND injury AND exercise' (1), none on how to get down; esearch-only leads are not citations; coach and manual pages for getting down from the bar. Fetched acefitness.org exercise-library/190/chin-ups -> 200; strengthlog.com/chin-up/ -> 200; strengthlog.com/pull-up/ -> 200; barbend.com/chin-up/ -> 200; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pull-up_(exercise) -> 200; darebee.com/exercises/pull-ups.html -> 200; inspireusafoundation.org/chin-ups/ -> 200; acefitness.org/resources/everyone/blog/6636/how-to-do-a-pull-up/ -> 200; verywellfit chin-up and pull-up pages -> 402; nerdfitness, garagegymreviews, healthline, menshealth, bodybuilding.com and puregym pull-up/chin-up pages -> 404; muscleandstrength.com chin-up and pull-up -> 403; nsca.com pull-ups -> 403; startingstrength.com chin-up -> 403; Body-Solid owner's manuals GDCC250, GDIP59, DPCC, GKR60 (bodysolid.com/content/...) -> 200 (assembly and general warnings only). No source says how to get down from the bar or fail a rep safely.

W2-8 2026-10-18: No card source gives a time for shoulder or elbow pain. NASM (re-fetched, 200) says only 'persists'. So the red-flag row fixes say 'Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.' with no time, and the time comes from the linked NHS boxes (shoulder: no better after two weeks; elbow: no better after a few weeks) (LR-28). The shrug and shoulder rows have no sourced link from the feeling to a cause: Bullbar names the shrug only as a fault, and Prinold 2016 (efetch) links arm position to impingement risk, not pain to a cause. So they read place + the source's fault + fix, with no 'usually means' (LR-6). The elbow rows keep 'usually means', because NASM links elbow tendon irritation to overuse.
